questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Arms of government and legislative powers
questions.concept: Removal of Senate President or Speaker
questions.stem: Under section 50(2)(c) of the 1999 Constitution, what legislative vote is required to remove the President of the Senate or the Speaker of the House of Representatives from office?

options.text: A simple majority of members present and voting
options.why: Routine bills pass by simple majority under s. 56(2), whereas removing presiding officers requires a two-thirds supermajority.
options.whyWrong: Routine bills pass by simple majority under s. 56(2), whereas removing presiding officers requires a two-thirds supermajority.

options.text: An executive order issued by the President
options.why: By separation of powers, the President cannot remove legislative presiding officers.
options.whyWrong: By separation of powers, the President cannot remove legislative presiding officers.

options.text: A resolution supported by at least two-thirds majority of the members of that House
options.why: Section 50(2)(c) requires a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds majority of the members of the respective House.

options.text: A petition signed by one-third of registered voters in Nigeria
options.why: Voters recall individual legislators in their own constituencies (s. 69), not presiding officers nationally.
options.whyWrong: Voters recall individual legislators in their own constituencies (s. 69), not presiding officers nationally.

questions.hint: Presiding officers hold constitutional leadership roles — a narrow simple majority is not enough to remove them.
questions.explanation: Under section 50(2)(c), the President or Deputy President of the Senate, or the Speaker or Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, vacates office if removed by a resolution of that House supported by not less than two-thirds majority of its members.
questions.trap: Because s. 50(1) elects presiding officers by simple majority, students often assume removal also needs only a simple majority.
questions.mnemonic: Simple majority elects the Speaker; two-thirds removes the Speaker.

askPresets.answer: Under section 50(2)(c), the President or Deputy President of the Senate, or the Speaker or Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, vacates office if removed by a resolution of that House supported by not less than two-thirds majority of its members.
Routine bills pass by simple majority under s. 56(2), whereas removing presiding officers requires a two-thirds supermajority.

questions.topic: Arms of government and legislative powers
questions.concept: Languages of the National Assembly
questions.stem: Under section 55 of the 1999 Constitution, the business of the National Assembly shall be conducted in English, and in which three Nigerian languages when adequate arrangements have been made?

options.text: Yoruba, Edo and Tiv
options.why: Edo and Tiv are not named in section 55.
options.whyWrong: Edo and Tiv are not named in section 55.

options.text: Hausa, Fulfulde and Kanuri
options.why: Section 55 names Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba rather than Fulfulde or Kanuri.
options.whyWrong: Section 55 names Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba rather than Fulfulde or Kanuri.

options.text: Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba
options.why: Section 55 expressly names English, and Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba when adequate arrangements have been made.

options.text: English only, with all indigenous languages barred
options.why: Section 55 explicitly includes Hausa, Igbo, and Yoruba once adequate arrangements exist.
options.whyWrong: Section 55 explicitly includes Hausa, Igbo, and Yoruba once adequate arrangements exist.

questions.hint: Think of the three major Nigerian languages expressly listed in section 55 (and section 97 for States).
questions.explanation: Section 55 states that the business of the National Assembly shall be conducted in English, and in Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba when adequate arrangements have been made therefor.
questions.trap: Because parliamentary debates take place in English in practice, many candidates wrongly assume the Constitution forbids indigenous languages.
questions.mnemonic: Section 55 lists English plus Hausa, Igbo, and Yoruba.

askPresets.answer: Section 55 states that the business of the National Assembly shall be conducted in English, and in Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba when adequate arrangements have been made therefor.
Section 55 explicitly includes Hausa, Igbo, and Yoruba once adequate arrangements exist.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Arms of government and checks and balances
questions.concept: President addressing National Assembly vs voting
questions.stem: Under section 67 of the 1999 Constitution, when the President addresses a joint sitting of the National Assembly or a Minister appears to explain ministry affairs, what are they constitutionally barred from doing?

options.text: Voting in either House or in any of its committees
options.why: Section 67(3) forbids any non-member (including the President or Ministers) from voting in either House or any committee.

options.text: Answering questions on budget proposals
options.why: Ministers attend specifically to explain the conduct of their Ministry when invited (s. 67(2)).
options.whyWrong: Ministers attend specifically to explain the conduct of their Ministry when invited (s. 67(2)).

options.text: Delivering a policy statement on national affairs
options.why: Delivering national policy addresses is expressly permitted under s. 67(1).
options.whyWrong: Delivering national policy addresses is expressly permitted under s. 67(1).

options.text: Presenting fiscal measures to lawmakers
options.why: Fiscal addresses are expressly permitted under section 67(1).
options.whyWrong: Fiscal addresses are expressly permitted under section 67(1).

questions.hint: Attendance and speech are allowed to coordinate government, yet separation of powers blocks casting ballots.
questions.explanation: Section 67 permits the President to address either House or a joint meeting (s. 67(1)) and requires Ministers to attend when invited to explain ministry affairs (s. 67(2)), while s. 67(3) strictly forbids any non-member from voting in the House or its committees.
questions.trap: Students know Ministers are summoned to parliament and sometimes confuse explaining ministry affairs with holding a legislative vote.
questions.mnemonic: President and Ministers may speak in Parliament (s. 67), never vote.

askPresets.answer: Section 67 permits the President to address either House or a joint meeting (s. 67(1)) and requires Ministers to attend when invited to explain ministry affairs (s. 67(2)), while s. 67(3) strictly forbids any non-member from voting in the House or its committees.
Ministers attend specifically to explain the conduct of their Ministry when invited (s. 67(2)).

questions.topic: Arms of government and legislative powers
questions.concept: Expenditure in default of Appropriation Act
questions.stem: If the financial year begins before the Appropriation Bill is passed into law, section 82 authorises the President to withdraw money from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for essential government services for up to

options.text: 6 months (or until the Appropriation Act starts, if earlier), capped proportionately at the previous year's Appropriation Act
options.why: Section 82 allows withdrawals for up to 6 months (or earlier enactment of the Act), not exceeding the proportionate amount authorised in the preceding financial year.

options.text: 3 months, at double the previous year's monthly rate
options.why: The maximum period is 6 months, capped proportionately at the previous year's authorised rate.
options.whyWrong: The maximum period is 6 months, capped proportionately at the previous year's authorised rate.

options.text: 12 months, without any spending ceiling
options.why: Unconstrained 12-month spending would bypass Parliament's power of the purse under ss. 80–81.
options.whyWrong: Unconstrained 12-month spending would bypass Parliament's power of the purse under ss. 80–81.

options.text: 21 days only, subject to Supreme Court approval
options.why: 21 days applies elsewhere; s. 82 grants up to 6 months capped by the preceding budget.
options.whyWrong: 21 days applies elsewhere; s. 82 grants up to 6 months capped by the preceding budget.

questions.hint: Think of half a financial year capped at last year's spending pace.
questions.explanation: Under section 82, if a new Appropriation Act is not yet in force when the financial year starts, the President may authorise necessary withdrawals from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for up to 6 months (or until the Act commences), capped proportionately at the preceding year's authorised rate.
questions.trap: 3 months (often confused with s. 146(2) election window) and 12 months are classic distractors against section 82's 6-month limit.
questions.mnemonic: Budget delay? President spends up to 6 months at last year's pace (s. 82).

askPresets.answer: Under section 82, if a new Appropriation Act is not yet in force when the financial year starts, the President may authorise necessary withdrawals from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for up to 6 months (or until the Act commences), capped proportionately at the preceding year's authorised rate.
The maximum period is 6 months, capped proportionately at the previous year's authorised rate.

questions.topic: Arms of government and checks and balances
questions.concept: Auditor-General independence and reporting
questions.stem: Under section 85(5)–(6) of the 1999 Constitution, to whom does the Auditor-General for the Federation submit audit reports on public accounts within 90 days of receiving the Accountant-General's financial statement?

options.text: The State Houses of Assembly exclusively
options.why: Federal public accounts go to the National Assembly; State Auditors-General report to State Houses of Assembly (s. 125).
options.whyWrong: Federal public accounts go to the National Assembly; State Auditors-General report to State Houses of Assembly (s. 125).

options.text: The Minister of Finance for private cabinet approval only
options.why: To protect legislative oversight over spending, reports go to the National Assembly rather than remaining inside the executive.
options.whyWrong: To protect legislative oversight over spending, reports go to the National Assembly rather than remaining inside the executive.

options.text: The Chairman of the ruling political party
options.why: Audit oversight is a constitutional legislative check, never a partisan party review.
options.whyWrong: Audit oversight is a constitutional legislative check, never a partisan party review.

options.text: Each House of the National Assembly, for consideration by its public accounts committee
options.why: Section 85(5) requires submission to each House of the National Assembly for public accounts committee review, while s. 85(6) guarantees independence.

questions.hint: Ask which branch holds the power of the purse and needs independent verification of how funds were spent.
questions.explanation: Section 85(5) directs the Auditor-General to submit audit reports within 90 days of receiving the Accountant-General's statement to each House of the National Assembly (for public accounts committees), and s. 85(6) shields the Auditor-General from outside control.
questions.trap: Because the Accountant-General sits in the Finance Ministry, students often assume the Auditor-General also reports only to the Finance Minister.
questions.mnemonic: Accountant-General keeps books; Auditor-General checks them and reports to Parliament.

askPresets.answer: Section 85(5) directs the Auditor-General to submit audit reports within 90 days of receiving the Accountant-General's statement to each House of the National Assembly (for public accounts committees), and s. 85(6) shields the Auditor-General from outside control.
To protect legislative oversight over spending, reports go to the National Assembly rather than remaining inside the executive.

questions.topic: Arms of government and legislative powers
questions.concept: Summoning witnesses and evidence under s. 89
questions.stem: During an investigation under section 88, what coercive power does section 89(1) grant a House or committee of the National Assembly to gather evidence?

options.text: Passing life prison sentences directly without court trial
options.why: Criminal conviction and imprisonment belong solely to the courts under section 6.
options.whyWrong: Criminal conviction and imprisonment belong solely to the courts under section 6.

options.text: Summoning any person in Nigeria to give evidence, examining witnesses on oath, and issuing a warrant to compel attendance if ignored
options.why: Section 89(1)(a)–(d) empowers the House/committee to procure evidence, examine witnesses on oath, summon anyone in Nigeria, and issue warrants on failure to attend.

options.text: Seizing private bank balances permanently without a court order
options.why: Legislative committees investigate and recommend; they do not exercise judicial forfeiture.
options.whyWrong: Legislative committees investigate and recommend; they do not exercise judicial forfeiture.

options.text: Dismissing Supreme Court Justices by committee resolution
options.why: Removing the CJN or Justices requires strict section 292 procedures.
options.whyWrong: Removing the CJN or Justices requires strict section 292 procedures.

questions.hint: Separate compelling testimony/evidence during an inquiry from imposing criminal punishment.
questions.explanation: Section 89(1) equips legislative inquiries with quasi-judicial evidence-gathering powers: procuring written/oral evidence, taking sworn testimony, summoning any person in Nigeria, and ordering warrants (enforceable by police) when a summons is ignored without just cause.
questions.trap: Students sometimes confuse the power to compel witnesses to attend (s. 89) with judicial power to try and convict.
questions.mnemonic: Section 89 compels witnesses and documents, not criminal convictions.

askPresets.answer: Section 89(1) equips legislative inquiries with quasi-judicial evidence-gathering powers: procuring written/oral evidence, taking sworn testimony, summoning any person in Nigeria, and ordering warrants (enforceable by police) when a summons is ignored without just cause.
Criminal conviction and imprisonment belong solely to the courts under section 6.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Arms of government and executive succession
questions.concept: Death or inability of President-elect
questions.stem: Under section 136(1) of the 1999 Constitution, if the person duly elected as President dies before taking the Oath of Allegiance and oath of office, what happens?

options.text: INEC cancels the entire election and holds a fresh presidential poll within 30 days
options.why: Section 136(2) calls a fresh election only if BOTH President-elect and Vice-President-elect die or cannot assume office; if only the President-elect dies, the VP-elect steps up.
options.whyWrong: Section 136(2) calls a fresh election only if BOTH President-elect and Vice-President-elect die or cannot assume office; if only the President-elect dies, the VP-elect steps up.

options.text: The outgoing President stays in office for another four years
options.why: The incumbent's tenure ends under s. 135; succession passes to the Vice-President-elect.
options.whyWrong: The incumbent's tenure ends under s. 135; succession passes to the Vice-President-elect.

options.text: The runner-up presidential candidate from the opposition party becomes President
options.why: An election ticket belongs to the winning President-elect and Vice-President-elect, never the runner-up.
options.whyWrong: An election ticket belongs to the winning President-elect and Vice-President-elect, never the runner-up.

options.text: The Vice-President-elect is sworn in as President and nominates a new Vice-President with approval by simple majority at a joint sitting of the National Assembly
options.why: Section 136(1) mandates swearing in the Vice-President-elect as President, who nominates a new Vice-President approved by simple majority of the National Assembly sitting jointly.

questions.hint: Remember that a President and Vice-President are elected on a joint ticket.
questions.explanation: Under section 136(1), if the President-elect dies or cannot be sworn in, the Vice-President-elect is sworn in as President and nominates a new Vice-President approved by a simple majority of the National Assembly at a joint sitting. Fresh elections (s. 136(2)) occur only if both die/cannot assume office.
questions.trap: Many candidates jump to 'fresh election' under s. 136(2), overlooking that s. 136(1) first elevates the Vice-President-elect.
questions.mnemonic: President-elect dies -> VP-elect becomes President (joint-sitting approval for new VP).

askPresets.answer: Under section 136(1), if the President-elect dies or cannot be sworn in, the Vice-President-elect is sworn in as President and nominates a new Vice-President approved by a simple majority of the National Assembly at a joint sitting. Fresh elections (s. 136(2)) occur only if both die/cannot assume office.
Section 136(2) calls a fresh election only if BOTH President-elect and Vice-President-elect die or cannot assume office; if only the President-elect dies, the VP-elect steps up.

questions.topic: Arms of government and checks and balances
questions.concept: Permanent incapacity procedure under s. 144
questions.stem: Under section 144 of the 1999 Constitution, removing a President for permanent incapacity of body or mind begins with a \frac{2}{3} resolution of the Federal Executive Council and verification by

options.text: an INEC medical verification committee
options.why: INEC conducts elections and party regulation, never presidential medical panels.
options.whyWrong: INEC conducts elections and party regulation, never presidential medical panels.

options.text: a panel of seven judges appointed by the Chief Justice of Nigeria
options.why: The Chief Justice's seven-person non-medical panel belongs to gross-misconduct impeachment under section 143, not medical incapacity under section 144.
options.whyWrong: The Chief Justice's seven-person non-medical panel belongs to gross-misconduct impeachment under section 143, not medical incapacity under section 144.

options.text: a simple majority vote of State Governors
options.why: State Governors have no constitutional vote in federal s. 144 incapacity proceedings.
options.whyWrong: State Governors have no constitutional vote in federal s. 144 incapacity proceedings.

options.text: a five-doctor medical panel appointed by the President of the Senate, including the President's personal physician
options.why: Section 144(1)(b) and (4) establish a five-practitioner medical panel appointed by the Senate President, one being the President's personal physician.

questions.hint: Contrast gross-misconduct impeachment (s. 143: CJN + 7 citizens) with medical incapacity (s. 144).
questions.explanation: Section 144 requires (1) a two-thirds resolution of all members of the Federal Executive Council declaring incapacity, and (2) verification by a five-doctor panel appointed by the Senate President (including the officeholder's personal physician), published in the Official Gazette.
questions.trap: Mixing up s. 143's 7-person CJN panel with s. 144's 5-doctor Senate President panel is a classic high-level JAMB trap.
questions.mnemonic: Impeachment (s. 143) = CJN 7-person panel; Incapacity (s. 144) = FEC + 5 doctors.

askPresets.answer: Section 144 requires (1) a two-thirds resolution of all members of the Federal Executive Council declaring incapacity, and (2) verification by a five-doctor panel appointed by the Senate President (including the officeholder's personal physician), published in the Official Gazette.
The Chief Justice's seven-person non-medical panel belongs to gross-misconduct impeachment under section 143, not medical incapacity under section 144.

questions.topic: Arms of government and executive succession
questions.concept: Dual vacancy succession to Senate President
questions.stem: If the offices of BOTH the President and the Vice-President become vacant at the same time under section 146(2) of the 1999 Constitution, who acts as President and for how long?

options.text: The Speaker of the House of Representatives, for the remainder of the 4-year term
options.why: Section 146(2) designates the President of the Senate (not the Speaker) and limits the interim period to 3 months.
options.whyWrong: Section 146(2) designates the President of the Senate (not the Speaker) and limits the interim period to 3 months.

options.text: The President of the Senate, for not more than 3 months pending an election of a new President
options.why: Section 146(2) assigns the presidency to the President of the Senate for not more than 3 months, during which a new President is elected for the unexpired term.

options.text: The Chief Justice of Nigeria, for 6 months
options.why: The head of the judiciary does not assume executive headship under section 146(2).
options.whyWrong: The head of the judiciary does not assume executive headship under section 146(2).

options.text: The Secretary to the Government of the Federation, for 1 year
options.why: The SGF is an appointed official, not in the constitutional line of succession.
options.whyWrong: The SGF is an appointed official, not in the constitutional line of succession.

questions.hint: Look to the head of the upper legislative chamber and the 90-day / 3-month special election clock.
questions.explanation: Under section 146(2), when both the President and Vice-President offices are vacant, the President of the Senate holds the office of President for not more than 3 months, during which INEC conducts an election for a new President to serve the unexpired term.
questions.trap: Students sometimes assume the Senate President finishes the whole remaining term rather than holding the seat for at most 3 months pending an election.
questions.mnemonic: Both vacant -> Senate President holds fort for at most 3 months.

askPresets.answer: Under section 146(2), when both the President and Vice-President offices are vacant, the President of the Senate holds the office of President for not more than 3 months, during which INEC conducts an election for a new President to serve the unexpired term.
Section 146(2) designates the President of the Senate (not the Speaker) and limits the interim period to 3 months.

questions.topic: Arms of government and executive powers
questions.concept: Attorney-General prosecution and nolle prosequi
questions.stem: Under section 174(1) of the 1999 Constitution, what unique constitutional power over federal criminal prosecutions does the Attorney-General of the Federation possess?

options.text: Trying and sentencing accused persons directly without a judge
options.why: Only courts try and sentence accused persons; the AGF prosecutes or discontinues.
options.whyWrong: Only courts try and sentence accused persons; the AGF prosecutes or discontinues.

options.text: Instituting, taking over, or discontinuing before judgment any federal criminal proceedings (except courts-martial)
options.why: Section 174(1)(a)–(c) empowers the Attorney-General to institute, take over, and discontinue (nolle prosequi) before judgment any federal criminal prosecution other than courts-martial.

options.text: Overruling Supreme Court appellate decisions after judgment
options.why: Section 174(1)(c) permits discontinuance only *before* judgment is delivered, never overruling a delivered judgment.
options.whyWrong: Section 174(1)(c) permits discontinuance only *before* judgment is delivered, never overruling a delivered judgment.

options.text: Granting pardons unilaterally without consulting the Council of State
options.why: Prerogative of mercy belongs to the President after consulting the Council of State under section 175.
options.whyWrong: Prerogative of mercy belongs to the President after consulting the Council of State under section 175.

questions.hint: Check when the Attorney-General can stop a criminal case — before judgment or after?
questions.explanation: Section 174(1) empowers the Attorney-General of the Federation to institute, take over, or discontinue at any stage *before judgment* any criminal case under an Act of the National Assembly (other than a court-martial), having regard to public interest, justice, and preventing abuse (s. 174(3)).
questions.trap: Note the two built-in limits students miss: discontinuance must happen *before judgment*, and *courts-martial* are excluded.
questions.mnemonic: AGF can start, take over, or stop federal prosecutions before judgment.

askPresets.answer: Section 174(1) empowers the Attorney-General of the Federation to institute, take over, or discontinue at any stage *before judgment* any criminal case under an Act of the National Assembly (other than a court-martial), having regard to public interest, justice, and preventing abuse (s. 174(3)).
Section 174(1)(c) permits discontinuance only *before* judgment is delivered, never overruling a delivered judgment.

questions.concept: Prerogative of mercy consultation
questions.stem: Under section 175(1)–(2) of the 1999 Constitution, before exercising the prerogative of mercy to grant a pardon or commute a punishment for a federal offence, the President must

options.text: obtain a two-thirds vote of the House of Representatives
options.why: Pardons do not go through a House of Representatives vote.
options.whyWrong: Pardons do not go through a House of Representatives vote.

options.text: consult with the Council of State
options.why: Section 175(2) requires the President to exercise prerogative-of-mercy powers after consultation with the Council of State (and in accordance with its advice for court-martial offences under s. 175(3)).

options.text: submit a referendum to voters in the convict's home State
options.why: Prerogative of mercy is never put to a referendum.
options.whyWrong: Prerogative of mercy is never put to a referendum.

options.text: gain consent from the Inspector-General of Police
options.why: The Police Force has no constitutional role in pardons.
options.whyWrong: The Police Force has no constitutional role in pardons.

questions.hint: Which advisory federal body includes former Presidents and Chief Justices alongside State Governors?
questions.explanation: Section 175(2) requires the President to consult the Council of State before granting pardons, respites, commutations, or remissions for federal statutory offences (and act on its advice for military court-martial offences under s. 175(3)).
questions.trap: Students know the President grants pardons yet often overlook the mandatory Council of State consultation in s. 175(2).
questions.mnemonic: Presidential pardon needs Council of State consultation (s. 175).

askPresets.answer: Section 175(2) requires the President to consult the Council of State before granting pardons, respites, commutations, or remissions for federal statutory offences (and act on its advice for military court-martial offences under s. 175(3)).
Pardons do not go through a House of Representatives vote.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Supreme Court original jurisdiction
questions.stem: Under section 232(1) of the 1999 Constitution, in which kind of case does the Supreme Court sit as a court of FIRST instance (exclusive original jurisdiction)?

options.text: Every armed robbery or murder trial nationwide
options.why: Section 232(2) proviso strictly forbids conferring *any* criminal original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court.
options.whyWrong: Section 232(2) proviso strictly forbids conferring *any* criminal original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court.

options.text: Any legal-right dispute between the Federation and a State, or between one State and another State
options.why: Section 232(1) gives the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction over disputes between the Federation and a State or between States involving legal rights.

options.text: Presidential election petitions
options.why: Presidential election petitions begin in the Court of Appeal under section 239(1), not the Supreme Court.
options.whyWrong: Presidential election petitions begin in the Court of Appeal under section 239(1), not the Supreme Court.

options.text: Landlord-tenant disputes in Abuja
options.why: Ordinary tenancy cases belong to Magistrate or High Courts, never Supreme Court original jurisdiction.
options.whyWrong: Ordinary tenancy cases belong to Magistrate or High Courts, never Supreme Court original jurisdiction.

questions.hint: Remember the federal umpire role of the Supreme Court when two governments clash.
questions.explanation: To resolve intergovernmental legal disputes neutrally at the apex, section 232(1) grants the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction in disputes involving legal rights between the Federation and a State or between States (while s. 232(2) bars criminal original jurisdiction).
questions.trap: Presidential election petitions are the biggest distractor here — remember they start at the Court of Appeal (s. 239) and reach the Supreme Court only on appeal.
questions.mnemonic: Supreme Court starts inter-government disputes (s. 232), never criminal trials or first-step election petitions.

askPresets.answer: To resolve intergovernmental legal disputes neutrally at the apex, section 232(1) grants the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction in disputes involving legal rights between the Federation and a State or between States (while s. 232(2) bars criminal original jurisdiction).
Presidential election petitions begin in the Court of Appeal under section 239(1), not the Supreme Court.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Federal High Court exclusive jurisdiction
questions.stem: Which specialized civil subject belongs exclusively to the Federal High Court under section 251(1) of the 1999 Constitution rather than a State High Court?

options.text: Civil cases involving Federal Government revenue, company taxation, customs duties, copyright, and admiralty
options.why: Section 251(1)(a)–(g) grants the Federal High Court exclusive jurisdiction over federal revenue, federal/company taxation, customs, CAMA/companies, copyright/patents, and admiralty.

options.text: Customary marriage inheritance inside a single village
options.why: Customary inheritance belongs to Customary or State Courts, not the Federal High Court.
options.whyWrong: Customary inheritance belongs to Customary or State Courts, not the Federal High Court.

options.text: Ordinary disputes between an individual bank customer and their local bank branch
options.why: The proviso to s. 251(1)(d) expressly excludes individual customer-bank disputes from Federal High Court exclusivity.
options.whyWrong: The proviso to s. 251(1)(d) expressly excludes individual customer-bank disputes from Federal High Court exclusivity.

options.text: Local tenancy rent arrears between two private neighbours
options.why: Private landlord-tenant claims sit in State Magistrate or High Courts.
options.whyWrong: Private landlord-tenant claims sit in State Magistrate or High Courts.

questions.hint: Check both what s. 251(1) covers and the famous customer-bank proviso in s. 251(1)(d)!
questions.explanation: Section 251(1) gives the Federal High Court exclusive civil jurisdiction over federal agencies/revenue, federal taxes, customs/excise, banking regulation/CBN, companies (CAMA), copyright/patents, and admiralty — while excluding ordinary individual customer-versus-bank disputes.
questions.trap: Because s. 251(1)(d) mentions 'banks', candidates often pick individual customer-bank disputes, missing the proviso that carves them out.
questions.mnemonic: Federal High Court handles federal revenue, taxes, customs, companies, copyright, and admiralty.

options.whyWrong: Automatic repeal of all prior laws would create a total legal vacuum; s. 315 kept existing laws valid subject to constitutional conformity.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Can a written constitution be flexible?
questions.stem: Which statement accurately explains the relationship between a 'written' constitution and a 'rigid' constitution?

options.text: Every written constitution is automatically rigid, and every unwritten constitution is flexible
options.why: Form (written vs unwritten) and amendment ease (rigid vs flexible) are separate classifications; a written constitution can in principle allow amendment by ordinary legislative process.
options.whyWrong: Form (written vs unwritten) and amendment ease (rigid vs flexible) are separate classifications; a written constitution can in principle allow amendment by ordinary legislative process.

options.text: Written refers to codification in a single document, while rigid refers to requiring a special amendment process harder than ordinary law-making
options.why: Written/unwritten classifies documentary form, whereas rigid/flexible classifies amendment difficulty; Nigeria's 1999 Constitution happens to be both written and rigid.

options.text: Unwritten constitutions contain zero written laws or statutes
options.why: Unwritten constitutions (such as Britain's) include major written statutes alongside conventions; they simply are not codified into one supreme document.
options.whyWrong: Unwritten constitutions (such as Britain's) include major written statutes alongside conventions; they simply are not codified into one supreme document.

options.text: Rigid constitutions can never be amended at all
options.why: Rigid means harder to amend than ordinary statutes (e.g. s. 9), not impossible to amend.
options.whyWrong: Rigid means harder to amend than ordinary statutes (e.g. s. 9), not impossible to amend.

questions.hint: Separate *how a constitution is written down* from *how it is amended*.
questions.explanation: Written vs unwritten describes whether core rules sit in one codified document (Nigeria, USA) or across statutes and usages (Britain). Rigid vs flexible describes whether amendments need a special procedure (Nigeria s. 9) or follow ordinary law-making (Britain).
questions.trap: Saying 'every written constitution is rigid' or 'unwritten means zero written words' are classic exam traps.
questions.mnemonic: Written = one book; Rigid = hard to change.

questions.concept: Why constitutional supremacy requires rigidity
questions.stem: Why do federal constitutions such as Nigeria's 1999 Constitution adopt a rigid amendment procedure rather than simple-majority amendment?

options.why: Rigid written constitutions actually strengthen judicial review by providing a clear supreme standard (ss. 1(3), 4(8)).
options.whyWrong: Rigid written constitutions actually strengthen judicial review by providing a clear supreme standard (ss. 1(3), 4(8)).

options.text: To protect the division of federal-state powers and fundamental rights from sudden alteration by a temporary parliamentary majority
options.why: Rigidity shields federal power distribution (s. 8, Second Schedule) and Chapter IV rights from hasty unilateral changes by one tier or a bare majority.

options.text: To abolish the need for periodic elections
options.why: Rigid constitutions entrench periodic elections rather than abolishing them.
options.whyWrong: Rigid constitutions entrench periodic elections rather than abolishing them.

questions.concept: Distinction between a constitution and constitutionalism
questions.stem: What is the key difference between merely having a 'constitution' and practising 'constitutionalism'?

options.text: A constitution applies to citizens only, whereas constitutionalism applies to judges only

options.whyWrong: Under s. 1(1), the Constitution binds all authorities and persons alike.

options.text: Constitutionalism means replacing written laws with unwritten customs only
options.why: Constitutionalism is about limited, rule-bound government, whether the constitution is written or unwritten.
options.whyWrong: Constitutionalism is about limited, rule-bound government, whether the constitution is written or unwritten.

options.text: Constitutionalism grants the executive unlimited emergency power forever
options.why: Unlimited arbitrary power is the opposite of constitutionalism.
options.whyWrong: Unlimited arbitrary power is the opposite of constitutionalism.

options.text: A constitution is the text of rules, whereas constitutionalism means government actually obeys and is limited by those supreme rules
options.why: A military junta or dictator may hold a paper constitution while ignoring it; constitutionalism means governing strictly within constitutional limits (s. 1(1)–(2)).

questions.hint: Contrast owning a rulebook with actually playing inside its boundaries.
questions.explanation: Constitutionalism (listed in JAMB Syllabus Part 1 Topic 9 and anchored in s. 1(1)–(3)) means government power is genuinely checked and exercised strictly under constitutional limits, rather than merely existing on paper.

questions.topic: Rule of law and fundamental human rights
questions.concept: Six lawful grounds for arrest or detention
questions.stem: Under section 35(1) of the 1999 Constitution, which ground does NOT justify depriving a person of personal liberty?

options.text: In execution of a sentence or order of a court after criminal conviction
options.why: Section 35(1)(a) expressly permits deprivation of liberty in execution of a criminal court sentence.
options.whyWrong: Section 35(1)(a) expressly permits deprivation of liberty in execution of a criminal court sentence.

options.text: To silence peaceful public criticism of a governor's budget
options.why: Silencing peaceful political criticism violates s. 39 (expression) and s. 35(1), which lists no ground for political dissent.

options.text: Upon reasonable suspicion of having committed a criminal offence
options.why: Section 35(1)(c) permits arrest upon reasonable suspicion of a criminal offence to bring the person before a court.
options.whyWrong: Section 35(1)(c) permits arrest upon reasonable suspicion of a criminal offence to bring the person before a court.

options.text: For care or treatment of a dangerous infectious disease or unsound mind under law
options.why: Section 35(1)(e) permits lawful detention for care, treatment, or community protection regarding infectious disease or unsound mind.
options.whyWrong: Section 35(1)(e) permits lawful detention for care, treatment, or community protection regarding infectious disease or unsound mind.

questions.hint: Spot the political abuse that falls completely outside section 35(1)(a)–(f).
questions.explanation: Section 35(1) limits deprivation of personal liberty strictly to procedure permitted by law across six enumerated grounds (court sentence, court order/legal obligation, criminal suspicion, minor's education/welfare, infectious disease/unsound mind/addiction, and unlawful entry/extradition). Political dissent is never a valid ground.
questions.trap: Public-health detention under s. 35(1)(e) sometimes surprises students, leading them to pick (d) instead of the clear rights abuse in (c).
questions.mnemonic: Section 35(1) lists 6 strict legal reasons for detention — never political speech.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Rule of law and fundamental human rights
questions.concept: Awaiting-trial detention cap
questions.stem: Under the proviso to section 35(1) of the 1999 Constitution, an accused person held in lawful custody awaiting trial shall NOT be detained for longer than

options.text: 10 years regardless of the charge
options.why: There is no fixed 10-year blanket rule; the ceiling is the maximum term prescribed for that specific offence.
options.whyWrong: There is no fixed 10-year blanket rule; the ceiling is the maximum term prescribed for that specific offence.

options.text: twice the maximum sentence for the offence
options.why: Detaining a pre-trial suspect longer than the maximum statutory penalty itself violates the s. 35(1) proviso.
options.whyWrong: Detaining a pre-trial suspect longer than the maximum statutory penalty itself violates the s. 35(1) proviso.

options.text: the maximum period of imprisonment prescribed for the offence charged
options.why: The proviso to s. 35(1) caps awaiting-trial detention at no longer than the maximum imprisonment term prescribed for the offence.

options.text: 24 hours in all cases
options.why: 24 hours is the written-reasons deadline (s. 35(3)) or nearby-court arraignment limit (s. 35(5)(a)), not the trial cap.
options.whyWrong: 24 hours is the written-reasons deadline (s. 35(3)) or nearby-court arraignment limit (s. 35(5)(a)), not the trial cap.

questions.hint: Imagine holding someone awaiting trial for 5 years on a minor charge whose maximum penalty is 6 months!
questions.explanation: The proviso to section 35(1) prevents indefinite awaiting-trial abuse by forbidding detention of any charged person in custody awaiting trial for longer than the maximum period of imprisonment prescribed for that offence.
questions.trap: Students often mix up the 24-hour / 2-month / 3-month clocks in s. 35(3)–(4) with the overall maximum-penalty ceiling in s. 35(1) proviso.
questions.mnemonic: Never detain an awaiting-trial suspect longer than the crime's maximum sentence.

askPresets.answer: The proviso to section 35(1) prevents indefinite awaiting-trial abuse by forbidding detention of any charged person in custody awaiting trial for longer than the maximum period of imprisonment prescribed for that offence.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Rule of law and fundamental human rights
questions.concept: Two-month vs three-month trial rule
questions.stem: Under section 35(4) of the 1999 Constitution, a person arrested on suspicion of a non-capital offence must be tried within what period (failing which they are released conditionally or unconditionally)?

options.text: 24 hours regardless of bail status
options.why: 24 hours is for written grounds (s. 35(3)) and nearby-court appearance (s. 35(5)(a)).
options.whyWrong: 24 hours is for written grounds (s. 35(3)) and nearby-court appearance (s. 35(5)(a)).

options.text: 6 months if in custody, or 12 months if on bail
options.why: The constitutional periods in s. 35(4) are 2 months and 3 months, not 6 and 12 months.
options.whyWrong: The constitutional periods in s. 35(4) are 2 months and 3 months, not 6 and 12 months.

options.text: 7 days if in custody, or 14 days if on bail
options.why: 1–2 days governs *first appearance* in court (s. 35(5)), whereas 2–3 months governs *trial* (s. 35(4)).
options.whyWrong: 1–2 days governs *first appearance* in court (s. 35(5)), whereas 2–3 months governs *trial* (s. 35(4)).

options.text: 2 months from arrest if in custody or not entitled to bail, or 3 months from arrest if released on bail
options.why: Section 35(4)(a)–(b) sets 2 months for persons in custody/not entitled to bail, and 3 months for persons released on bail.

questions.hint: Notice the shorter 2-month deadline protects suspects still sitting in custody without bail.
questions.explanation: Section 35(4) requires bringing an arrested suspect to court within a reasonable time and trying them within 2 months if held in custody or denied bail (s. 35(4)(a)), or 3 months if released on bail (s. 35(4)(b)) — excluding capital offences (s. 35(7)(a)).
questions.trap: Mixing up 'bringing before a court' (1–2 days, s. 35(5)) with 'starting trial' (2–3 months, s. 35(4)) is a classic JAMB trap.
questions.mnemonic: See judge in 1–2 days; start trial in 2 months (custody) or 3 months (bail).

askPresets.answer: Section 35(4) requires bringing an arrested suspect to court within a reasonable time and trying them within 2 months if held in custody or denied bail (s. 35(4)(a)), or 3 months if released on bail (s. 35(4)(b)) — excluding capital offences (s. 35(7)(a)).
1–2 days governs *first appearance* in court (s. 35(5)), whereas 2–3 months governs *trial* (s. 35(4)).

questions.concept: Capital offence exception in s. 35(7)
questions.stem: Section 35(7)(a) expressly states that the 2-month and 3-month bail/trial release deadlines in section 35(4) do NOT apply to a person arrested or detained upon reasonable suspicion of

options.text: having committed a capital offence
options.why: Section 35(7)(a) exempts persons arrested or detained upon reasonable suspicion of having committed a capital offence from s. 35(4).

options.text: a minor traffic parking violation
options.why: Minor offences fall squarely within s. 35(4)'s bail and trial protections.
options.whyWrong: Minor offences fall squarely within s. 35(4)'s bail and trial protections.

options.text: breaching a private civil contract
options.why: Civil contract debts do not fall under criminal suspicion, let alone capital exemptions.
options.whyWrong: Civil contract debts do not fall under criminal suspicion, let alone capital exemptions.

options.text: criticising a municipal tax rate
options.why: Peaceful expression is protected under s. 39.
options.whyWrong: Peaceful expression is protected under s. 39.

questions.explanation: While section 35(4) entitles non-capital suspects to release if not tried within 2 or 3 months, section 35(7)(a) carves out persons detained on reasonable suspicion of having committed a capital offence (alongside short ≤ 3-month military/police disciplinary detention in s. 35(7)(b)).
questions.trap: Students sometimes forget that s. 35(7)(a) excludes capital offences from automatic s. 35(4) release, though fair hearing within a reasonable time (s. 36(4)) still applies.
questions.mnemonic: Capital offences sit outside s. 35(4)'s automatic 2- or 3-month release.

questions.topic: Rule of law and fundamental human rights
questions.concept: Administrative tribunal fairness under s. 36(2)
questions.stem: Under section 36(2) of the 1999 Constitution, a statute conferring power on a government authority to decide questions affecting a citizen's civil rights is valid ONLY if the law

options.text: requires the citizen to pay a deposit before reading the decision
options.why: No such fee condition appears in section 36(2).
options.whyWrong: No such fee condition appears in section 36(2).

options.text: makes the minister's decision final, conclusive, and unchallengeable in court
options.why: Final-and-conclusive clauses barring court review violate section 36(2)(b) and section 4(8).
options.whyWrong: Final-and-conclusive clauses barring court review violate section 36(2)(b) and section 4(8).

options.text: allows the agency to punish citizens secretly without hearing their side
options.why: Refusing prior representation violates audi alteram partem under section 36(2)(a).
options.whyWrong: Refusing prior representation violates audi alteram partem under section 36(2)(a).

options.text: gives affected persons an opportunity to make representations beforehand AND contains no clause making the authority's decision final and conclusive
options.why: Section 36(2)(a)–(b) requires both prior opportunity to make representations and no finality clause shutting out judicial review.

questions.hint: Look for the two twin pillars of natural justice and judicial review in section 36(2).
questions.explanation: Section 36(2) lets administrative bodies decide routine regulatory issues only if the law (a) lets affected persons make representations before the decision, and (b) contains no provision making the authority's decision final and conclusive against the courts.
questions.trap: Many students assume all administrative rulings are final unless appealed to another minister; s. 36(2)(b) preserves access to courts.
questions.mnemonic: Hear the person first, and never bar the courts (s. 36(2)).

askPresets.answer: Section 36(2) lets administrative bodies decide routine regulatory issues only if the law (a) lets affected persons make representations before the decision, and (b) contains no provision making the authority's decision final and conclusive against the courts.

questions.concept: Accused rights: free interpreter and defence
questions.stem: Under section 36(6)(e) of the 1999 Constitution, if a person charged with a criminal offence cannot understand the language used at the trial, they are entitled to

options.text: hire an interpreter entirely at their own expense
options.why: The Constitution explicitly requires the interpreter to be provided *without payment*.
options.whyWrong: The Constitution explicitly requires the interpreter to be provided *without payment*.

options.text: have, without payment, the assistance of an interpreter
options.why: Section 36(6)(e) guarantees the assistance of an interpreter *without payment* if the accused cannot understand the language used at trial.

options.text: have the trial conducted solely in the accused's dialect without records
options.why: The court provides an interpreter free of charge rather than suspending formal court records.
options.whyWrong: The court provides an interpreter free of charge rather than suspending formal court records.

options.text: waive their right to cross-examine prosecution witnesses
options.why: Section 36(6)(d) separately guarantees the right to examine prosecution witnesses.
options.whyWrong: Section 36(6)(d) separately guarantees the right to examine prosecution witnesses.

questions.explanation: Section 36(6) gives every criminal defendant five core rights: prompt notice in an understood language, adequate time and facilities to prepare defence, self-defence or counsel of choice, witness examination on equal terms, and a free interpreter.
questions.trap: Hiring an interpreter at the accused's own cost is a classic distractor — s. 36(6)(e) specifies *without payment*.
questions.mnemonic: Free interpreter guaranteed if you do not understand the court language.

questions.concept: Right to copy of judgment and unwritten offence bar
questions.stem: Under section 36(11) and (12) of the 1999 Constitution, a criminal defendant cannot be compelled to give evidence at trial, and a person cannot be convicted of a criminal offence unless

options.text: that offence is defined and its penalty is prescribed in a written law
options.why: Section 36(12) strictly prohibits convicting anyone of an offence unless it is defined and its penalty prescribed in a written law (Act, State Law, or subsidiary instrument).

options.text: a community leader declares the act shameful
options.why: Unwritten customary or moral disapproval cannot support a criminal conviction under s. 36(12).
options.whyWrong: Unwritten customary or moral disapproval cannot support a criminal conviction under s. 36(12).

options.text: the prosecutor requests an unwritten penalty
options.why: Both the offence AND its penalty must appear in a written law under s. 36(12).
options.whyWrong: Both the offence AND its penalty must appear in a written law under s. 36(12).

options.text: the police chief issues an oral warning
options.why: Oral warnings do not constitute written criminal statutes.
options.whyWrong: Oral warnings do not constitute written criminal statutes.

questions.hint: Remember the rule against unwritten customary crimes in Nigerian criminal justice.
questions.explanation: Section 36(11) protects the accused against compelled self-incrimination at trial, while section 36(12) mandates that no person shall be convicted of a criminal offence unless that offence is defined and the penalty therefor is prescribed in a written law.
questions.trap: Students sometimes forget that *both* the crime's definition and its penalty must be written down before conviction is valid.
questions.mnemonic: No written crime and written penalty, no criminal conviction (s. 36(12)).

questions.concept: Right to privacy in s. 37
questions.stem: Which elements are explicitly guaranteed and protected under section 37 (Right to private and family life) of the 1999 Constitution?

options.text: Immunity from disclosing assets to the Code of Conduct Bureau
options.why: Public officers must declare assets under the Fifth Schedule.

options.whyWrong: Public budgets are subject to legislative and audit scrutiny under ss. 80–85, not personal privacy.

options.text: Privacy of citizens, their homes, correspondence, telephone conversations and telegraphic communications

questions.concept: Religious freedom in schools and secret society ban
questions.stem: Under section 38(2) and (4) of the 1999 Constitution, freedom of thought, conscience, and religion includes

options.text: banning religious communities from teaching pupils in wholly community-maintained schools
options.why: Section 38(3) expressly protects religious instruction by a community in schools maintained wholly by that community.
options.whyWrong: Section 38(3) expressly protects religious instruction by a community in schools maintained wholly by that community.

options.text: the right to join a secret society on campus as a protected religion
options.why: Section 38(4) expressly states that nothing in section 38 entitles anyone to form, participate in, or belong to a secret society.
options.whyWrong: Section 38(4) expressly states that nothing in section 38 entitles anyone to form, participate in, or belong to a secret society.

options.why: Compelling students into religious worship of another faith without parent/guardian approval violates s. 38(2).
options.whyWrong: Compelling students into religious worship of another faith without parent/guardian approval violates s. 38(2).

options.text: freedom from being forced in any school to take religious instruction or ceremonies of another religion not approved by one's parent or guardian — while barring secret societies
options.why: Section 38(2) protects pupils from unapproved religious instruction/ceremonies, and s. 38(4) excludes any right to form or join a secret society.

questions.stem: Under section 39(3) of the 1999 Constitution, freedom of expression does NOT invalidate a law reasonably justifiable in a democratic society that

options.text: prevents disclosure of confidential information, upholds court independence, or restricts government officials, armed forces, and police
options.why: Section 39(3)(a)–(b) allows democratic laws protecting confidential info, court authority, broadcast regulation, and restrictions on public/armed/police/security personnel.

options.text: bans citizens from criticising election results peacefully
options.why: Peaceful political criticism by citizens is core protected speech under s. 39(1).
options.whyWrong: Peaceful political criticism by citizens is core protected speech under s. 39(1).

options.text: closes down all private newspapers indefinitely without court order
options.why: Shutting newspapers arbitrarily violates s. 39(1)–(2) and rule of law.
options.whyWrong: Shutting newspapers arbitrarily violates s. 39(1)–(2) and rule of law.

options.text: punishes reporters for quoting parliamentary debates accurately
options.why: Reporting public legislative proceedings is lawful under free expression.
options.whyWrong: Reporting public legislative proceedings is lawful under free expression.

questions.explanation: Section 39(3) permits laws reasonably justifiable in a democratic society to protect official confidences, maintain court authority and independence, regulate broadcasting/films, and restrict expression by government, armed forces, police, and security personnel.

questions.concept: Extradition and criminal travel limits
questions.stem: Under section 41(2) of the 1999 Constitution, when may a democratic law validly restrict a Nigerian citizen's freedom of movement or permit removing them to another country?

options.text: To banish political opponents permanently from Nigeria
options.why: Section 41(1) flatly forbids expelling Nigerian citizens for political reasons.
options.whyWrong: Section 41(1) flatly forbids expelling Nigerian citizens for political reasons.

options.text: To prevent a criminal suspect from leaving Nigeria, or for trial/imprisonment abroad under a reciprocal agreement
options.why: Section 41(2)(a)–(b) allows democratic laws restricting suspects' exit or removing persons to a country with a reciprocal agreement for trial or sentence.

options.text: To force all unemployed youths to remain inside their birth villages
options.why: Citizens may reside in any part of Nigeria under section 41(1).
options.whyWrong: Citizens may reside in any part of Nigeria under section 41(1).

options.text: To hand citizens over to any foreign country even without a reciprocal treaty
options.why: The proviso to s. 41(2)(b) explicitly requires a reciprocal agreement between Nigeria and the receiving country.
options.whyWrong: The proviso to s. 41(2)(b) explicitly requires a reciprocal agreement between Nigeria and the receiving country.

questions.hint: Check the proviso at the end of section 41(2)(b) on extradition agreements.

questions.stem: Under section 30(1) and (2) of the 1999 Constitution, how does deprivation of citizenship differ between a citizen by *registration* and a citizen by *naturalisation*?

options.text: Both can be deprived for 3-year imprisonment within 7 years

options.whyWrong: Section 30(1) applies the 3-year imprisonment rule ONLY to naturalised citizens ('other than a person who is a citizen of Nigeria by birth or by registration').

options.whyWrong: This reverses section 30(1), which protects citizens by registration from the 7-year prison-sentence clause.

options.whyWrong: Both registered (under s. 30(2)) and naturalised (under s. 30(1)–(2)) citizens can be deprived on stated grounds.

options.why: 15 years residence and Governor's attestation apply to naturalisation (s. 27(2)(d), (g)), not registration (s. 26).
options.whyWrong: 15 years residence and Governor's attestation apply to naturalisation (s. 27(2)(d), (g)), not registration (s. 26).

options.text: Being born inside Nigeria before 1960
options.why: Birth in Nigeria before 1960 relates to citizenship by birth under s. 25(1)(a).
options.whyWrong: Birth in Nigeria before 1960 relates to citizenship by birth under s. 25(1)(a).

options.text: Being a member of a registered political party
options.why: Political party membership is never required to acquire citizenship.
options.whyWrong: Political party membership is never required to acquire citizenship.

15 years residence and Governor's attestation apply to naturalisation (s. 27(2)(d), (g)), not registration (s. 26).

questions.concept: Periodic review of constituencies by INEC
questions.stem: Under sections 73 and 74 of the 1999 Constitution, how often must INEC review the division of States and the Federation into Senatorial districts and Federal constituencies, and when does an alteration take effect?

options.text: Every 4 years, approved by the Supreme Court
options.why: Intervals are at least 10 years, approved by each House of the National Assembly under s. 73(2).
options.whyWrong: Intervals are at least 10 years, approved by each House of the National Assembly under s. 73(2).

options.text: Every 2 years, taking effect immediately in the middle of the current legislative term
options.why: Mid-term boundary changes are barred by s. 74; intervals are at least 10 years.
options.whyWrong: Mid-term boundary changes are barred by s. 74; intervals are at least 10 years.

options.text: At intervals of not less than 10 years (or after a census), taking effect only after the dissolution of the House then in existence
options.why: Section 73 requires review at intervals of not less than 10 years (or following a national census), and s. 74 delays any alteration until the current House is dissolved.

options.text: Only once at independence in 1960
options.why: Constituency boundaries are reviewed periodically to keep populations nearly equal (s. 72).
options.whyWrong: Constituency boundaries are reviewed periodically to keep populations nearly equal (s. 72).

questions.hint: Look at why a sitting House finishes its term under existing boundaries before new maps take effect.
questions.explanation: Under section 73, INEC reviews Senatorial districts and Federal constituencies at intervals of not less than 10 years (or after a census under s. 73(2)), and section 74 prevents mid-term disruption by making alterations take effect only after the dissolution of the sitting House.

questions.concept: Death or withdrawal leaving a single candidate
questions.stem: Under section 132(3) of the 1999 Constitution, if after the close of nominations for a Presidential election only ONE candidate remains due to disqualification, withdrawal, incapacitation, disappearance, or death of the other candidates, what must INEC do?

options.text: Postpone the election for 4 years
options.why: Extending nomination time is a brief statutory extension, not a 4-year postponement.
options.whyWrong: Extending nomination time is a brief statutory extension, not a 4-year postponement.

options.text: Declare the surviving single candidate President without voting
options.why: Section 132(3) requires extending nomination time rather than crowning an unopposed survivor without reopening nominations.
options.whyWrong: Section 132(3) requires extending nomination time rather than crowning an unopposed survivor without reopening nominations.

options.text: Extend the time for nomination
options.why: Section 132(3) obliges INEC to extend the time for nomination so other parties can field candidates.

options.text: Appoint the runner-up from the previous election
options.why: Previous runners-up have no claim to current nominations.
options.whyWrong: Previous runners-up have no claim to current nominations.

questions.explanation: Section 132(3) directs INEC to extend the time for nomination whenever disqualification, withdrawal, incapacitation, disappearance, or death leaves only one candidate after nominations close (distinct from a sole nominated candidate under s. 133).

questions.mnemonic: If rivals vanish after nomination closes, INEC extends nomination time (s. 132(3)).

questions.topic: The electoral process and presidential elections
questions.concept: Third presidential election rule in s. 134(5)
questions.stem: Under section 134(4)–(5) of the 1999 Constitution, if the second presidential run-off election between two candidates ALSO fails to produce a candidate with both majority and 25% in \frac{2}{3} of States and FCT, how is the third election decided?

options.text: By drawing lots at the Supreme Court
options.why: The Supreme Court never decides presidential ties by lot.
options.whyWrong: The Supreme Court never decides presidential ties by lot.

options.text: By a joint vote of the Senate and House of Representatives
options.why: The National Assembly no longer serves as an electoral college for the President (unlike the unamended 1979 draft or 1963 system); s. 134(5) uses popular simple majority.
options.whyWrong: The National Assembly no longer serves as an electoral college for the President (unlike the unamended 1979 draft or 1963 system); s. 134(5) uses popular simple majority.

options.text: By a simple majority of votes cast at the third election arranged within 21 days (removing the State spread requirement)
options.why: Section 134(5) directs INEC to hold another election between the two candidates within 21 days, where a simple majority of votes cast elects the President.

options.text: By appointing the candidate with more votes in Abuja alone
options.why: Section 134(5) uses nationwide simple majority of votes cast.
options.whyWrong: Section 134(5) uses nationwide simple majority of votes cast.

questions.hint: Notice how Nigeria's 1999 Constitution avoids a parliamentary electoral college in the final round!
questions.explanation: Under section 134(5), if the two-candidate second election under s. 134(4) still fails the 25%-in-two-thirds spread hurdle, INEC arranges a third election within 21 days between the same two candidates, won purely by a majority of votes cast.
questions.trap: Students recalling older 1979 debates often think deadlock goes to an electoral college in the National Assembly; in 1999 s. 134(5), voters decide by simple majority.
questions.mnemonic: 1st & 2nd polls need 25% spread; 3rd poll uses simple majority (s. 134(5)).

options.whyWrong: Dual citizenship acquired by birth is protected under section 28(1) and does not trigger disqualification under s. 66(1)(a) or s. 137(1)(a).

options.text: Changing political parties 5 years before the election
options.why: Changing parties prior to nomination does not disqualify future candidacy.
options.whyWrong: Changing parties prior to nomination does not disqualify future candidacy.

options.text: Presenting a forged certificate to INEC, or being convicted and sentenced for dishonesty or Code of Conduct breach within the past 10 years
options.why: Sections 66(1)(d), (i) and 137(1)(e), (j) explicitly disqualify anyone presenting a forged certificate to INEC or convicted/sentenced for dishonesty or Code of Conduct contravention within 10 years.

options.text: Being under 40 years old
options.why: Under Fourth Alteration No. 27, 25 (House) and 35 (Senate/President) are sufficient ages.
options.whyWrong: Under Fourth Alteration No. 27, 25 (House) and 35 (Senate/President) are sufficient ages.

questions.hint: Check the integrity disqualifications in sections 66(1) and 137(1).
questions.explanation: Sections 66(1) and 137(1) bar candidates who voluntarily acquired non-birth foreign citizenship, are of unsound mind, under death/dishonesty sentence, convicted of dishonesty or Code of Conduct breach within 10 years, undischarged bankrupts, secret-society members, indicted for fraud, or who presented a forged certificate to INEC.

options.text: 14 days from the date of the occurrence of the event, decision, or action complained of

options.whyWrong: Pre-election suits must be filed quickly before general polling, within 14 days of the event.

questions.concept: Electoral systems: simple majority vs proportional representation
questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes a Simple Majority (Plurality) electoral system from Proportional Representation?

options.text: Under Simple Majority, the candidate with the highest single vote total wins the seat even with under 50%, whereas Proportional Representation allocates seats in proportion to party vote shares
options.why: Simple majority awards each constituency seat to the highest vote-getter (even below 50%), while proportional representation distributes seats according to each party's percentage of votes.

options.text: Under Simple Majority, voters cannot vote for individual candidates
options.why: Voters choose individual constituency candidates in simple majority, whereas party lists are common in proportional representation.
options.whyWrong: Voters choose individual constituency candidates in simple majority, whereas party lists are common in proportional representation.

options.text: Proportional Representation guarantees every winner gets over 50% in single-member seats
options.why: Single-member >50% winners define the Absolute Majority system, not proportional representation.
options.whyWrong: Single-member >50% winners define the Absolute Majority system, not proportional representation.

options.whyWrong: Simple majority tends to produce clear single-party majorities compared with coalition-prone proportional representation.

questions.hint: Compare plurality (most votes wins one seat) with proportionality (seat share matches vote share).
questions.explanation: In a Simple Majority (First-Past-The-Post) system, whichever candidate gets more votes than any rival wins the seat even below half of total votes. questions.topic: The electoral process and governorship elections
questions.concept: Sole governorship candidate YES/NO test
questions.stem: Under section 179(1) of the 1999 Constitution, if only ONE candidate is nominated for a State Governorship election, how is that candidate declared duly elected?

options.text: Automatically without any ballot box opening
options.why: Even a sole candidate must pass a YES/NO ballot plus LGA spread under s. 179(1).
options.whyWrong: Even a sole candidate must pass a YES/NO ballot plus LGA spread under s. 179(1).

options.text: By winning a majority of YES votes over NO votes AND at least \frac{1}{4} of votes in at least \frac{2}{3} of all LGAs in the State
options.why: Section 179(1)(a)–(b) requires both more YES than NO votes and at least 25% of votes in at least two-thirds of all LGAs in the State (failing which fresh nominations are called).

options.text: By a confirmation vote of the State House of Assembly
options.why: Governors are directly elected by voters under s. 178(5) and s. 179(1).
options.whyWrong: Governors are directly elected by voters under s. 178(5) and s. 179(1).

options.text: By winning a majority of YES votes in the State capital LGA only
options.why: Spread across at least two-thirds of all LGAs in the State is still required.
options.whyWrong: Spread across at least two-thirds of all LGAs in the State is still required.

questions.hint: Even when unopposed, voters get YES vs NO — and the spread rule still applies!

options.why: Jurisdictional objections are judicial questions decided by the tribunal at final judgment, never by INEC.
options.whyWrong: Jurisdictional objections are judicial questions decided by the tribunal at final judgment, never by INEC.

options.text: Pause the entire trial for 12 months while appeals run to the Supreme Court
options.why: Section 285(8) was enacted specifically to stop preliminary objections from stalling the 180-day trial.
options.whyWrong: Section 285(8) was enacted specifically to stop preliminary objections from stalling the 180-day trial.

options.text: Suspend its ruling on the preliminary objection and deliver it at the stage of final judgment
options.why: Section 285(8) requires the tribunal or court to suspend its ruling on preliminary/interlocutory jurisdiction objections and deliver it at final judgment.

options.why: Automatic dismissal on mere filing would defeat substantive justice.
options.whyWrong: Automatic dismissal on mere filing would defeat substantive justice.

options.whyWrong: Trade unions are pressure groups/associations, distinct from political parties under ss. 40 and 221.

options.whyWrong: Campus clubs are associations under s. 40, not political parties unless engaged in electoral vote-canvassing and registered.

options.why: Commercial partnerships do not canvass votes for public elections.
options.whyWrong: Commercial partnerships do not canvass votes for public elections.

options.whyWrong: Allowing partisan rival auditors would compromise neutrality; s. 225(6) requires auditors who are not members of any political party.

options.whyWrong: Advocating environmental protection (cf. s. 20) via peaceful association (s. 40) is completely lawful.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Anomic vs associational pressure groups
questions.stem: In Gabriel Almond's classification taught in Nigerian Government curricula, what distinguishes an *anomic* pressure group from an *associational* pressure group?

options.text: Anomic groups register with INEC as political parties
options.why: Anomic groups have no permanent registration or electoral structure.
options.whyWrong: Anomic groups have no permanent registration or electoral structure.

options.text: Anomic groups sit inside the military and civil service hierarchy
options.why: Groups existing inside state institutions (bureaucracies, military) are *institutional* pressure groups.
options.whyWrong: Groups existing inside state institutions (bureaucracies, military) are *institutional* pressure groups.

options.text: Associational groups are based strictly on blood kinship with no formal rules
options.why: Kinship, ethnic, and traditional ties with informal structures describe *non-associational* groups.
options.whyWrong: Kinship, ethnic, and traditional ties with informal structures describe *non-associational* groups.

options.text: Anomic groups erupt spontaneously in unorganised protests or riots over sudden grievances, whereas associational groups have formal organisation, offices, and paid or elected officers
options.why: Associational groups (unions, chambers) are formally organised and permanent; anomic groups arise spontaneously and often outside formal channels.

questions.hint: Notice the Greek root of 'anomic' (unstructured/spontaneous) vs 'associational' (formal association).
questions.explanation: Almond's fourfold typology separates associational groups (formal trade unions and professional bodies), institutional groups (inside state organs), non-associational groups (informal kinship/ethnic ties), and anomic groups (spontaneous, unorganised street protests or riots).
questions.trap: Mixing up 'institutional' (inside government) with 'anomic' (spontaneous outburst) is a classic exam mix-up.
questions.mnemonic: Associational = formal union; Institutional = inside state; Non-associational = kinship; Anomic = sudden outburst.

Groups existing inside state institutions (bureaucracies, military) are *institutional* pressure groups.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Mandatory Abuja headquarters under s. 222(f)
questions.stem: Why does section 222(f) of the 1999 Constitution require every Nigerian political party to locate its headquarters in the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja?

options.text: Because Abuja is the only city where voting is allowed
options.why: All 36 States and the FCT vote equally in national elections.
options.whyWrong: All 36 States and the FCT vote equally in national elections.

options.text: To reinforce national identity and ensure parties do not function as regional bodies anchored in a single State
options.why: Requiring Abuja headquarters alongside national logos and open membership (s. 222(b), (e)–(f)) prevents regionalised parties.

options.text: So the Minister of FCT can appoint party leaders
options.why: Parties elect their own officers democratically every ≤ 4 years under s. 223.
options.whyWrong: Parties elect their own officers democratically every ≤ 4 years under s. 223.

options.text: Because State capitals forbid political party offices
options.why: Parties operate State, LGA, and ward branches nationwide alongside their Abuja national HQ.
options.whyWrong: Parties operate State, LGA, and ward branches nationwide alongside their Abuja national HQ.

questions.hint: Connect s. 222(f) with Nigeria's historical effort to move away from ethnic-regional parties.
questions.explanation: Working together with s. 222(b) (open membership) and s. 222(e) (no ethnic/religious/regional symbols), s. 222(f) anchors every party's national headquarters in neutral Federal Capital Territory, Abuja, promoting national integration.
questions.trap: Having national headquarters in Abuja does NOT stop parties from opening branches across all 36 States.
questions.mnemonic: Abuja HQ keeps parties national, while branches operate nationwide.

askPresets.answer: Working together with s. 222(b) (open membership) and s. 222(e) (no ethnic/religious/regional symbols), s. 222(f) anchors every party's national headquarters in neutral Federal Capital Territory, Abuja, promoting national integration.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Party primaries and convention monitoring
questions.stem: Under Third Schedule Part I Item F paragraph 15(c) of the 1999 Constitution, what role does INEC play regarding internal political party conventions, congresses, and primaries?

options.text: Writing each party's campaign manifesto
options.why: Parties draft their own manifestos conforming to Chapter II (s. 224).
options.whyWrong: Parties draft their own manifestos conforming to Chapter II (s. 224).

options.text: Hand-picking every party's presidential flagbearer personally
options.why: Party members/delegates select candidates at primaries; INEC monitors compliance with constitutional and statutory rules.
options.whyWrong: Party members/delegates select candidates at primaries; INEC monitors compliance with constitutional and statutory rules.

options.text: Monitoring the organisation and operation of political parties, including their finances, conventions, congresses and party primaries
options.why: Paragraph 15(c) explicitly empowers INEC to monitor the organisation and operation of political parties, including their finances, conventions, congresses, and primaries.

options.text: Replacing party executive committees every 6 months
options.why: Parties elect executives every ≤ 4 years under s. 223.
options.whyWrong: Parties elect executives every ≤ 4 years under s. 223.

questions.hint: Think of an umpire observing internal party selection to make sure rules are obeyed.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 15(c) of Part I of the Third Schedule gives INEC constitutional authority to monitor political parties' organisation and operations — specifically including their finances, conventions, congresses, and primaries — to uphold internal democracy under s. 223.
questions.trap: Monitoring primaries means observing compliance, never choosing candidates for parties.
questions.mnemonic: INEC monitors party conventions, primaries, and books (3rd Sched. para. 15(c)).

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Open membership criteria in s. 222(b)
questions.stem: Section 222(b) of the 1999 Constitution guarantees that membership of any registered political party must be open to every citizen of Nigeria irrespective of

options.text: place of origin, circumstance of birth, sex, religion, or ethnic grouping
options.why: Section 222(b) verbatim forbids excluding any Nigerian citizen by place of origin, circumstance of birth, sex, religion, or ethnic grouping.

options.text: minimum voter registration age or citizenship itself
options.why: Party members are Nigerian citizens (and non-citizens have no constitutional right to join Nigerian political parties under s. 222(b)).
options.whyWrong: Party members are Nigerian citizens (and non-citizens have no constitutional right to join Nigerian political parties under s. 222(b)).

options.text: whether the member belongs to two rival parties at once
options.why: Party constitutions typically forbid simultaneous membership in rival parties.
options.whyWrong: Party constitutions typically forbid simultaneous membership in rival parties.

options.text: whether the person is serving a prison sentence for electoral fraud
options.why: Electoral laws and party rules regulate eligibility and conduct.
options.whyWrong: Electoral laws and party rules regulate eligibility and conduct.

questions.hint: Notice the exact five non-discrimination grounds listed in section 222(b).
questions.explanation: Section 222(b) ensures every registered political party is a truly national civic body open to every citizen of Nigeria regardless of place of origin, circumstance of birth, sex, religion, or ethnic grouping.
questions.trap: Because s. 222(b) says 'every citizen of Nigeria', non-citizens are excluded even though origin, sex, faith, and ethnicity cannot bar any Nigerian.
questions.mnemonic: Party doors stay open to all Nigerians regardless of origin, birth, sex, faith, or tribe.
