questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Resigning seat upon joining a statutory commission
questions.stem: Under section 68(1)(e) of the 1999 Constitution, what happens if a serving member of the House of Representatives accepts appointment as a member of a Federal Commission established by the Constitution (such as INEC or FCC)?

options.text: The legislator transfers the House seat to a family member
options.why: Legislative seats are never hereditary or transferable; INEC conducts a by-election.
options.whyWrong: Legislative seats are never hereditary or transferable; INEC conducts a by-election.

options.text: The legislator holds both the House seat and an INEC seat simultaneously
options.why: Serving inside independent commissions like INEC while sitting in Parliament violates s. 68(1)(e) and s. 156.
options.whyWrong: Serving inside independent commissions like INEC while sitting in Parliament violates s. 68(1)(e) and s. 156.

options.text: The legislator vacates the legislative seat (save as otherwise prescribed by the Constitution)
options.why: Section 68(1)(e) vacates the seat of any Senator or Representative who becomes a member of a constitutional or statutory commission (save where the Constitution prescribes ex-officio legislative membership).

options.text: The commission becomes part of the House of Representatives
options.why: Commissions retain their separate constitutional status.
options.whyWrong: Commissions retain their separate constitutional status.

questions.hint: Check section 68(1)(e) right next to the ministerial-appointment rule in s. 68(1)(d).
questions.explanation: Just as s. 68(1)(d) vacates a legislator's seat upon becoming a Minister, Commissioner, or Special Adviser, s. 68(1)(e) vacates the seat if the member joins a constitutional or statutory commission or body (unless the Constitution specifically places legislators on it).
questions.trap: Students know ministers cannot stay legislators yet often forget s. 68(1)(e) also bars holding statutory commissions simultaneously.
questions.mnemonic: Join a Cabinet or Commission -> vacate your legislative seat (s. 68(1)(d)–(e)).

askPresets.answer: Just as s. 68(1)(d) vacates a legislator's seat upon becoming a Minister, Commissioner, or Special Adviser, s. 68(1)(e) vacates the seat if the member joins a constitutional or statutory commission or body (unless the Constitution specifically places legislators on it).
Serving inside independent commissions like INEC while sitting in Parliament violates s. 68(1)(e) and s. 156.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Main operational difference between parties and pressure groups
questions.stem: What is the fundamental functional difference between a political party and a pressure group?

options.text: Pressure groups exist only in unitary states
options.why: Pressure groups operate actively in both federal and unitary democracies under freedom of association.
options.whyWrong: Pressure groups operate actively in both federal and unitary democracies under freedom of association.

options.text: Pressure groups draft the Constitution, while political parties run courts
options.why: Courts are run by the judiciary (s. 6), not political parties.
options.whyWrong: Courts are run by the judiciary (s. 6), not political parties.

options.text: Political parties cannot publish manifestos, while pressure groups can
options.why: Parties publish programmes conforming to Chapter II (s. 224).
options.whyWrong: Parties publish programmes conforming to Chapter II (s. 224).

options.text: Political parties nominate candidates and seek to win and exercise government power, whereas pressure groups seek to influence government policy without seeking office
options.why: Political parties contest elections to control government (ss. 65, 221, 229), while pressure groups lobby and persuade policymakers to protect specific interests or causes.

questions.hint: Ask which organisation puts candidates on the ballot to govern, and which stays outside to press demands.
questions.explanation: Under both political theory and Nigeria's Constitution (ss. 40, 221, 229), political parties exist to sponsor candidates, win elections, and form or control government, whereas pressure groups (trade unions, professional bodies, advocacy coalitions) seek to influence public policy in their members' or cause's favour.
questions.trap: Notice how simple the test is: control government = political party; influence government = pressure group.
questions.mnemonic: Parties seek power; pressure groups seek influence.

askPresets.answer: Under both political theory and Nigeria's Constitution (ss. 40, 221, 229), political parties exist to sponsor candidates, win elections, and form or control government, whereas pressure groups (trade unions, professional bodies, advocacy coalitions) seek to influence public policy in their members' or cause's favour.
Parties publish programmes conforming to Chapter II (s. 224).

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Forfeiting registration for zero seats
questions.stem: A newly registered political party fields candidates in a general election yet fails to win a single National Assembly seat, State Assembly seat, chairmanship ward, or councillorship seat, and fails to score 25% in any State or LGA. Under section 225A, what may INEC do?

options.text: Impose a 10-year prison sentence on every party voter
options.why: Voters are never punished for how they vote.
options.whyWrong: Voters are never punished for how they vote.

options.text: Merge the party forcibly into the winning party
options.why: INEC de-registers non-performing parties under s. 225A; mergers are voluntary party decisions.
options.whyWrong: INEC de-registers non-performing parties under s. 225A; mergers are voluntary party decisions.

options.text: Award the party a bonus seat in the Senate
options.why: Nigeria uses single-member plurality elections with no bonus seats for losing parties.
options.whyWrong: Nigeria uses single-member plurality elections with no bonus seats for losing parties.

options.text: De-register the political party
options.why: Section 225A(b)–(c) empowers INEC to de-register a party that fails to win 25% in at least one State (Presidential) or LGA (Governorship), OR fails to win at least one ward, Assembly seat, or Councillorship seat.

questions.hint: Recall the Fourth Alteration (No. 9) Act 2017 power given to INEC.
questions.explanation: Under section 225A (inserted by Fourth Alteration No. 9 Act 2017), failing all minimum electoral performance bars — 25% in 1 State (Presidential) or 1 LGA (Governorship), or winning 1 chairmanship ward, 1 National or State Assembly seat, or 1 councillorship seat — empowers INEC to de-register the party.
questions.trap: Students sometimes think INEC must wait for a party to breach Abuja-HQ or finance rules before de-registering it, missing the electoral-threshold clause in s. 225A(b)–(c).
questions.mnemonic: Zero seats and zero 25% footholds -> INEC can de-register under s. 225A.

askPresets.answer: Under section 225A (inserted by Fourth Alteration No. 9 Act 2017), failing all minimum electoral performance bars — 25% in 1 State (Presidential) or 1 LGA (Governorship), or winning 1 chairmanship ward, 1 National or State Assembly seat, or 1 councillorship seat — empowers INEC to de-register the party.
INEC de-registers non-performing parties under s. 225A; mergers are voluntary party decisions.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Indivisible and indissoluble Federation in s. 2
questions.stem: Section 2(1)–(2) of the 1999 Constitution describes Nigeria as

options.text: a loose confederation of autonomous regions free to secede unilaterally
options.why: Unilateral secession and confederal sovereignty are excluded by section 2(1)'s 'indivisible and indissoluble' clause.
options.whyWrong: Unilateral secession and confederal sovereignty are excluded by section 2(1)'s 'indivisible and indissoluble' clause.

options.text: one indivisible and indissoluble Sovereign State, and a Federation consisting of States and a Federal Capital Territory
options.why: Section 2(1)–(2) verbatim declares Nigeria one indivisible and indissoluble Sovereign State and a Federation consisting of States and a Federal Capital Territory.

options.text: a unitary state with no constitutionally protected sub-national legislatures
options.why: Section 2(2) and section 4(6) establish a federation with protected State Houses of Assembly.
options.whyWrong: Section 2(2) and section 4(6) establish a federation with protected State Houses of Assembly.

options.text: a protectorate administered under British Crown decrees
options.why: Nigeria became independent in 1960 and a sovereign Republic in 1963.
options.whyWrong: Nigeria became independent in 1960 and a sovereign Republic in 1963.

questions.hint: Recall the exact twin adjectives in section 2(1) defining Nigeria's territorial unity.
questions.explanation: Section 2(1) anchors national unity by declaring Nigeria 'one indivisible and indissoluble Sovereign State', while section 2(2) defines its constitutional structure as a Federation consisting of States and a Federal Capital Territory.
questions.trap: Students sometimes confuse a federation (no unilateral secession under s. 2(1)) with a confederation where member states may withdraw.
questions.mnemonic: Section 2: indivisible, indissoluble Federation of States and FCT.

askPresets.answer: Section 2(1) anchors national unity by declaring Nigeria 'one indivisible and indissoluble Sovereign State', while section 2(2) defines its constitutional structure as a Federation consisting of States and a Federal Capital Territory.
Unilateral secession and confederal sovereignty are excluded by section 2(1)'s 'indivisible and indissoluble' clause.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Federalism in Nigeria and FCT Abuja
questions.concept: Application of Constitution to FCT under s. 299
questions.stem: Under section 299 of the 1999 Constitution, the Constitution applies to the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja as if it were one of the States — meaning legislative and executive powers for the FCT vest in

options.text: an elected FCT State Governor and FCT State House of Assembly
options.why: The FCT has no State Governor or State House of Assembly; s. 299 vests those roles in the President and National Assembly.
options.whyWrong: The FCT has no State Governor or State House of Assembly; s. 299 vests those roles in the President and National Assembly.

options.text: the National Assembly (legislative) and the President (executive, via the FCT Minister)
options.why: Section 299(a) vests FCT legislative powers in the National Assembly, executive powers in the President (exercised via the FCT Minister under s. 302), and judicial powers in FCT courts.

options.text: the Governor of neighbouring Niger State
options.why: FCT Abuja is federal territory separate from all 36 States.
options.whyWrong: FCT Abuja is federal territory separate from all 36 States.

options.text: the six Area Council Chairmen jointly acting as federal legislators
options.why: The six Area Councils administer local council duties, while the National Assembly legislates for the FCT under s. 299(a).
options.whyWrong: The six Area Councils administer local council duties, while the National Assembly legislates for the FCT under s. 299(a).

questions.hint: Ask who acts as Abuja's 'Governor' and 'State House of Assembly' under section 299.
questions.explanation: Under sections 299 and 302, FCT Abuja is treated as if it were a State, with the National Assembly acting as its legislature, the President acting as its executive (typically delegating administration to the Minister of the FCT), and FCT High/Sharia/Customary courts exercising judicial power.
questions.trap: Because s. 299 says 'as if it were one of the States', candidates often assume Abuja elects a Governor and State House of Assembly.
questions.mnemonic: For FCT Abuja: NASS = State Assembly; President = Governor (s. 299).

askPresets.answer: Under sections 299 and 302, FCT Abuja is treated as if it were a State, with the National Assembly acting as its legislature, the President acting as its executive (typically delegating administration to the Minister of the FCT), and FCT High/Sharia/Customary courts exercising judicial power.
The FCT has no State Governor or State House of Assembly; s. 299 vests those roles in the President and National Assembly.

questions.topic: Federalism in Nigeria and legislative lists
questions.concept: Concurrent Legislative List items
questions.stem: Which set of subjects appears on the CONCURRENT Legislative List (Part II of the Second Schedule) where both the National Assembly and State Houses of Assembly may make laws?

options.text: Allocation of public revenue, antiquities and monuments, archives, tax collection, and university, technological and post-primary education
options.why: Part II of the Second Schedule places revenue allocation, antiquities, archives, collection of taxes, and university/technological/post-primary education on the Concurrent List.

options.text: Currency, coinage, defence, and external affairs
options.why: Currency, defence, and external affairs sit solely on the Exclusive Legislative List (Part I).
options.whyWrong: Currency, defence, and external affairs sit solely on the Exclusive Legislative List (Part I).

options.text: Citizenship, immigration, deportation, and extradition
options.why: Citizenship, immigration, deportation, and extradition are Exclusive List items (Items 9, 18, 27, 30).
options.whyWrong: Citizenship, immigration, deportation, and extradition are Exclusive List items (Items 9, 18, 27, 30).

options.text: Aviation, copyright, and naval forces
options.why: Aviation, copyright, and defence are Exclusive List items (Items 3, 13, 17).
options.whyWrong: Aviation, copyright, and defence are Exclusive List items (Items 3, 13, 17).

questions.hint: Pick the shared subjects that involve both federal standards and state institutions.
questions.explanation: Part II of the Second Schedule (Concurrent Legislative List) sets out shared federal-state legislative fields including division of public revenue, antiquities, archives, tax collection, electoral law for LGs, industrial/agricultural development, scientific research, and university/technological/post-primary education.
questions.trap: Remember that *primary* education falls under local council participation with States (Fourth Schedule para. 2(a)), while *university and post-primary* education sit on the Concurrent List.
questions.mnemonic: Concurrent List = shared taxes, revenue, archives, research, and higher/post-primary schools.

questions.concept: Exclusive vs Concurrent labour and census
questions.stem: Where do 'Census' and 'Labour, including trade unions and prescribing a national minimum wage' sit in the Second Schedule to the 1999 Constitution?

options.text: Both are residual matters outside the Constitution
options.why: Both are expressly enumerated in Part I of the Second Schedule.
options.whyWrong: Both are expressly enumerated in Part I of the Second Schedule.

options.text: Both sit on the Fourth Schedule for Local Government Councils
options.why: Neither national census nor national minimum wage belongs to local councils.
options.whyWrong: Neither national census nor national minimum wage belongs to local councils.

options.why: Labour and national minimum wage are explicitly listed in Item 34 of the Exclusive Legislative List.
options.whyWrong: Labour and national minimum wage are explicitly listed in Item 34 of the Exclusive Legislative List.

options.text: Both sit on the Exclusive Legislative List (Part I, Items 8 and 34)
options.why: Item 8 (Census) and Item 34 (Labour, trade unions, industrial disputes, national minimum wage) are both on the Exclusive Legislative List.

questions.explanation: Items 8 and 34 of Part I of the Second Schedule assign Census (including universal birth/death registration machinery) and Labour (including trade unions, industrial relations, and prescribing a national minimum wage) exclusively to the National Assembly.

questions.mnemonic: National minimum wage and Census are both Exclusive (Items 34 and 8).

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Boundary adjustment vs new State creation
questions.stem: How does adjusting the boundary of an existing State under section 8(2) differ from creating an entirely new State under section 8(1)?

options.text: Boundary adjustment requires a two-thirds referendum across all 36 States
options.why: Referendums are required for creating a *new State* (s. 8(1)(b)) or *new LGA* (s. 8(3)(b)), NOT for boundary adjustments (s. 8(2), (4)).
options.whyWrong: Referendums are required for creating a *new State* (s. 8(1)(b)) or *new LGA* (s. 8(3)(b)), NOT for boundary adjustments (s. 8(2), (4)).

options.text: Boundary adjustment requires a four-fifths vote of the Supreme Court
options.why: Boundary adjustment is a legislative process under s. 8(2), not a judicial vote.
options.whyWrong: Boundary adjustment is a legislative process under s. 8(2), not a judicial vote.

options.text: Boundary adjustment requires simple majorities in each House of the National Assembly and affected State Assemblies WITHOUT a referendum or nationwide State approvals
options.why: After the initial two-thirds area request (s. 8(2)(a)), boundary adjustment under s. 8(2)(b) needs only simple majorities in each House of the National Assembly and the affected State House(s) of Assembly.

options.text: Only the President may redraw State lines unilaterally by decree
options.why: Section 8(2) vests State boundary adjustment in an Act of the National Assembly following local requests and Assembly votes.
options.whyWrong: Section 8(2) vests State boundary adjustment in an Act of the National Assembly following local requests and Assembly votes.

questions.hint: Compare s. 8(1) (creating a new State) with s. 8(2) (adjusting an existing boundary).
questions.explanation: Section 8 makes creating a new State (s. 8(1)) far harder than adjusting an existing boundary (s. 8(2)): boundary adjustment starts with a two-thirds request from the demanding and affected areas, then passes by simple majorities in each House of the National Assembly and affected State House(s) of Assembly — with no referendum.
questions.trap: Candidates frequently confuse State creation (referendum + majority of all States + two-thirds NASS) with boundary adjustment (no referendum, simple majorities).
questions.mnemonic: New State = referendum + two-thirds NASS; Boundary tweak = simple majorities, no referendum.

askPresets.answer: Section 8 makes creating a new State (s. 8(1)) far harder than adjusting an existing boundary (s. 8(2)): boundary adjustment starts with a two-thirds request from the demanding and affected areas, then passes by simple majorities in each House of the National Assembly and affected State House(s) of Assembly — with no referendum.
Referendums are required for creating a *new State* (s. 8(1)(b)) or *new LGA* (s. 8(3)(b)), NOT for boundary adjustments (s. 8(2), (4)).

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Six principles for Federation Account formula
questions.stem: When the National Assembly determines the revenue-allocation formula from the Federation Account under section 162(2), which set of principles must it take into account (alongside ≥ 13% derivation)?

options.text: Number of political parties registered in each State
options.why: Party counts play zero role in revenue allocation.
options.whyWrong: Party counts play zero role in revenue allocation.

options.text: Population, equality of States, internal revenue generation, land mass, terrain, and population density
options.why: Section 162(2) explicitly lists population, equality of States, internal revenue generation, land mass, terrain, and population density.

options.text: Personal wealth of State Governors
options.why: Governors' private assets are irrelevant to public revenue sharing.
options.whyWrong: Governors' private assets are irrelevant to public revenue sharing.

options.text: Military base count in each geopolitical zone
options.why: Military installations are not among the s. 162(2) allocation criteria.
options.whyWrong: Military installations are not among the s. 162(2) allocation criteria.

questions.hint: Recall the six fairness criteria balancing population size, geography, and tax effort in section 162(2).
questions.explanation: Section 162(2) instructs the National Assembly (after presidential proposals advised by RMAFC) to apply especially population, equality of States, internal revenue generation, land mass, terrain, and population density, plus the ≥ 13% natural-resource derivation proviso.
questions.trap: Students know 'population' and 'derivation' yet often overlook 'internal revenue generation' and 'terrain' in section 162(2).
questions.mnemonic: Section 162(2) weighs people, State equality, tax effort, land, terrain, density, and ≥ 13% derivation.

askPresets.answer: Section 162(2) instructs the National Assembly (after presidential proposals advised by RMAFC) to apply especially population, equality of States, internal revenue generation, land mass, terrain, and population density, plus the ≥ 13% natural-resource derivation proviso.
Military installations are not among the s. 162(2) allocation criteria.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Grants-in-aid and set-off of State debts
questions.stem: Under sections 164 and 166 of the 1999 Constitution, the Federation may make grants-in-aid to supplement a State's revenue on National Assembly terms, AND what may the Federation do under section 166 if a State fails to repay sums owed to the Federation?

options.text: Dissolve the State's House of Assembly immediately
options.why: Debt default never authorises dissolving a State legislature.
options.whyWrong: Debt default never authorises dissolving a State legislature.

options.text: Set off the amount owed against any sums payable to that State under revenue allocation
options.why: Section 166 empowers the Federation to set off unpaid State loans or guarantees against Federation Account or statutory payments due to that State.

options.text: Sell the State's local council markets by auction
options.why: Markets are local assets; s. 166 uses fiscal set-off against statutory allocations.
options.whyWrong: Markets are local assets; s. 166 uses fiscal set-off against statutory allocations.

options.text: Abolish the State's Governorship seat
options.why: Elected offices cannot be abolished for fiscal arrears.
options.whyWrong: Elected offices cannot be abolished for fiscal arrears.

questions.hint: Look at the financial accounting mechanism called 'Set-off' in section 166.
questions.explanation: Section 164 allows federal grants-in-aid to States (and foreign states/international bodies under s. 164(2)), while section 166 protects federal loans by allowing set-off against revenue allocations payable to a defaulting State.
questions.trap: Set-off is a quiet fiscal clause in Chapter VI Part I C that tests careful reading of intergovernmental finance.
questions.mnemonic: Section 164 grants help States; s. 166 deducts unpaid debts at source.

askPresets.answer: Section 164 allows federal grants-in-aid to States (and foreign states/international bodies under s. 164(2)), while section 166 protects federal loans by allowing set-off against revenue allocations payable to a defaulting State.
Debt default never authorises dissolving a State legislature.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: RMAFC constitutional functions in Third Schedule
questions.stem: Which constitutional body advises the President on Federation Account revenue allocation proposals and determines appropriate remuneration for political officeholders and judicial officers?

options.text: The National Population Commission
options.why: The National Population Commission conducts censuses and vital registration (Item J).
options.whyWrong: The National Population Commission conducts censuses and vital registration (Item J).

options.text: The Federal Character Commission
options.why: The Federal Character Commission monitors equitable representation in public appointments (Item C).
options.whyWrong: The Federal Character Commission monitors equitable representation in public appointments (Item C).

options.text: The Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission (RMAFC)
options.why: Third Schedule Part I Item N paragraph 32 empowers RMAFC to monitor accruals/disbursements from the Federation Account, advise on allocation formulas, and determine remuneration for political and judicial officeholders.

options.text: The Code of Conduct Bureau
options.why: The Code of Conduct Bureau handles public officers' asset declarations and ethics (Item A).
options.whyWrong: The Code of Conduct Bureau handles public officers' asset declarations and ethics (Item A).

questions.hint: Look for the commission whose name explicitly pairs Revenue Mobilisation, Allocation, and Fiscal policy.
questions.explanation: Established under section 153(1)(n) and Third Schedule Part I Item N (para. 32), RMAFC monitors Federation Account inflows/disbursements, reviews revenue allocation principles, advises federal and state governments on fiscal efficiency, and determines political and judicial officers' remuneration.
questions.trap: Candidates know RMAFC advises on revenue sharing yet often miss its constitutional duty to fix salaries/allowances for political and judicial officers.
questions.mnemonic: RMAFC handles Federation Account sharing AND political/judicial pay.

askPresets.answer: Established under section 153(1)(n) and Third Schedule Part I Item N (para. 32), RMAFC monitors Federation Account inflows/disbursements, reviews revenue allocation principles, advises federal and state governments on fiscal efficiency, and determines political and judicial officers' remuneration.
The Federal Character Commission monitors equitable representation in public appointments (Item C).

questions.concept: Federal Character Commission mandate
questions.stem: Under Third Schedule Part I Item C paragraph 8 of the 1999 Constitution, what enforcement duty belongs to the Federal Character Commission?

options.text: Auditing private political party accounts
options.why: Auditing political parties belongs to INEC under ss. 225–226.
options.whyWrong: Auditing political parties belongs to INEC under ss. 225–226.

options.text: Fixing interest rates for commercial banks
options.why: Banking and currency belong to the Central Bank under federal banking statutes.
options.whyWrong: Banking and currency belong to the Central Bank under federal banking statutes.

options.text: Supervising local government elections
options.why: Local council elections are run by each State's SIEC.
options.whyWrong: Local council elections are run by each State's SIEC.

options.text: Working out an equitable formula for distributing posts in Federal and State public services and prosecuting heads of ministries or agencies who breach it
options.why: Paragraph 8(1)(a)–(c) empowers the Federal Character Commission to design equitable post-distribution formulas, promote/monitor/enforce compliance, and take legal measures (including prosecution) against non-complying heads.

questions.hint: Remember the Commission that turns section 14(3) diversity into enforceable hiring rules.
questions.explanation: Established by s. 153(1)(c) and Third Schedule Part I Item C, the Federal Character Commission works out equitable formulas for public-service posts and socio-economic amenities, enforces compliance with s. 14(3)–(4), and can prosecute violating agency heads.
questions.trap: Students often treat Federal Character as merely an unenforceable slogan, forgetting the Commission has explicit enforcement and prosecution powers in paragraph 8(1)(c).
questions.mnemonic: Federal Character Commission sets equitable formulas and enforces hiring compliance.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Criteria for defining Local Government areas
questions.stem: Under section 7(2) of the 1999 Constitution, when prescribing the geographical area over which a Local Government Council exercises authority, regard must be paid to

options.text: common interest of the community, traditional association of the community, and administrative convenience
options.why: Section 7(2)(b)(i)–(iii) expressly requires paying regard to common community interest, traditional association, and administrative convenience.

options.text: which political party won the previous governorship poll there
options.why: Partisan voting patterns are never a constitutional criterion for drawing local government areas.
options.whyWrong: Partisan voting patterns are never a constitutional criterion for drawing local government areas.

options.text: equal landmass in square kilometres regardless of people
options.why: Strict equal-area geometry is never mandated; community ties and convenience govern.
options.whyWrong: Strict equal-area geometry is never mandated; community ties and convenience govern.

options.text: distance from international airports
options.why: Airport distance has no place in section 7(2).
options.whyWrong: Airport distance has no place in section 7(2).

questions.hint: Check the three practical community criteria listed in section 7(2)(b).
questions.explanation: Section 7(2) directs the authority defining a local council's area to define it clearly and ensure regard is paid to (i) common interest of the community, (ii) traditional association of the community, and (iii) administrative convenience.
questions.trap: Equal area or equal population ignores the traditional-association and community-interest criteria written into s. 7(2)(b).
questions.mnemonic: LG borders look at common interest, traditional ties, and convenience (s. 7(2)).

askPresets.answer: Section 7(2) directs the authority defining a local council's area to define it clearly and ensure regard is paid to (i) common interest of the community, (ii) traditional association of the community, and (iii) administrative convenience.
Strict equal-area geometry is never mandated; community ties and convenience govern.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Economic planning board duty in s. 7(3)
questions.stem: Under section 7(3) of the 1999 Constitution, how are Local Government Councils constitutionally linked to State economic planning and development?

options.text: Every State House of Assembly must establish by Law an economic planning board in which local government councils participate
options.why: Section 7(3) makes it a duty of local councils to participate in economic planning and development, directing the State House of Assembly to establish an economic planning board by Law.

options.text: Local councils submit local budgets directly to the United Nations
options.why: Economic planning occurs inside the State-local constitutional framework, never via the UN.
options.whyWrong: Economic planning occurs inside the State-local constitutional framework, never via the UN.

options.text: Each council chairman sits inside the Senate Finance Committee
options.why: Council chairmen do not sit in the federal Senate.
options.whyWrong: Council chairmen do not sit in the federal Senate.

options.text: States are barred from involving local councils in development plans
options.why: Section 7(3) mandates local council participation, not exclusion.
options.whyWrong: Section 7(3) mandates local council participation, not exclusion.

questions.hint: Look at the statutory planning body required by section 7(3).
questions.explanation: Section 7(3) requires local government councils to participate in economic planning and development of their areas, and mandates each State House of Assembly to enact a Law establishing an economic planning board to facilitate that participation.
questions.trap: Students know local councils run markets and clinics yet often overlook their s. 7(3) constitutional planning role.
questions.mnemonic: Section 7(3): State Assembly sets up an economic planning board with local councils.

askPresets.answer: Section 7(3) requires local government councils to participate in economic planning and development of their areas, and mandates each State House of Assembly to enact a Law establishing an economic planning board to facilitate that participation.

questions.concept: Voter and candidate parity in s. 7(4)
questions.stem: Section 7(4) of the 1999 Constitution guarantees that every person entitled to vote or be voted for at an election to a State House of Assembly

options.text: can vote only if owning taxed land inside the council
options.why: Property qualifications do not exist in Nigeria's universal adult suffrage.
options.whyWrong: Property qualifications do not exist in Nigeria's universal adult suffrage.

options.text: must be at least 35 years old before contesting for local councillor
options.why: Section 106(b) sets State House of Assembly candidacy at 25 (and voter registration at 18 under s. 117(2)), so s. 7(4) carries those rights to local council polls.
options.whyWrong: Section 106(b) sets State House of Assembly candidacy at 25 (and voter registration at 18 under s. 117(2)), so s. 7(4) carries those rights to local council polls.

options.text: loses the right to vote in presidential elections
options.why: Voting in local polls never forfeits federal voting rights.
options.whyWrong: Voting in local polls never forfeits federal voting rights.

options.text: shall also have the right to vote or be voted for at an election to a Local Government Council
options.why: Section 7(4) secures voting and candidacy parity between State House of Assembly elections and Local Government Council elections.

questions.hint: Notice how s. 7(4) ties Local Government election rights directly to State House of Assembly qualifications.
questions.explanation: Section 7(4) binds every State Government to ensure that anyone qualified to vote (18+, s. 117(2)) or be voted for (25+, s. 106) at a State House of Assembly election holds the same right in a Local Government Council election.
questions.trap: Because local governments are regulated by State Laws under s. 7(1), students sometimes forget s. 7(4) stops States from imposing steeper age or property bars.
questions.mnemonic: Section 7(4): State Assembly voter/candidate rights carry straight to local councils.

questions.concept: Local council licensing and regulatory duties
questions.stem: Which set of local regulatory and licensing duties appears under paragraph 1(d) and (k) of the Fourth Schedule to the 1999 Constitution?

options.text: Licensing bicycles, hand trucks, canoes, wheelbarrows and carts; and regulating outdoor advertising, shops, kiosks, restaurants, bakeries, laundries and liquor sales
options.why: Fourth Schedule para. 1(d) covers non-mechanically propelled vehicles/canoes/carts, and para. 1(k) covers outdoor advertising, pets, shops/kiosks, food places, laundries, and liquor licensing.

options.text: Licensing commercial passenger aircraft and ocean tankers
options.why: Aviation and maritime shipping sit on the Exclusive Legislative List (Items 3 and 36).
options.whyWrong: Aviation and maritime shipping sit on the Exclusive Legislative List (Items 3 and 36).

options.text: Issuing national drivers' licences and international passports
options.why: Passports/immigration and federal trunk-road vehicle policy fall outside Fourth Schedule local cart/bicycle licensing.
options.whyWrong: Passports/immigration and federal trunk-road vehicle policy fall outside Fourth Schedule local cart/bicycle licensing.

options.text: Regulating commercial banks and stock exchanges
options.why: Banking and capital issues sit on the Exclusive Legislative List (Items 6 and 12).
options.whyWrong: Banking and capital issues sit on the Exclusive Legislative List (Items 6 and 12).

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: How State shares among its Local Councils under s. 162(8)
questions.stem: Once allocations enter a State Joint Local Government Account under section 162(6), who prescribes the terms and manner for distributing the amount standing to the credit of the local councils within that State?

options.text: The Independent National Electoral Commission
options.why: INEC handles elections and parties, not local fiscal sharing.
options.whyWrong: INEC handles elections and parties, not local fiscal sharing.

options.text: The Governor alone by verbal instruction
options.why: Section 162(8) requires terms prescribed by the State House of Assembly, not unilateral verbal orders.
options.whyWrong: Section 162(8) requires terms prescribed by the State House of Assembly, not unilateral verbal orders.

options.text: The House of Assembly of that State
options.why: Section 162(8) states that the amount standing to the credit of local government councils of a State shall be distributed among them on such terms and in such manner as may be prescribed by the House of Assembly of the State.

options.text: The Supreme Court Chief Registrar
options.why: Court registrars manage judicial administration, not revenue allocation.
options.whyWrong: Court registrars manage judicial administration, not revenue allocation.

questions.hint: Compare who sets national sharing (National Assembly, s. 162(3)–(5)) with who sets intra-State sharing among LGCs (s. 162(8)).
questions.explanation: Section 162 splits fiscal rules neatly across tiers: the National Assembly prescribes how the Federation Account splits among Federal, States, and LGCs (s. 162(3)–(5)), while each State House of Assembly prescribes how the local allocation inside that State is distributed among its local councils (s. 162(8)).
questions.trap: Students know the National Assembly passes federal revenue formulas and often miss that State Houses of Assembly govern intra-State LGC distribution under s. 162(8).
questions.mnemonic: NASS shares among tiers (s. 162(3)); State Assembly shares among its LGCs (s. 162(8)).

askPresets.answer: Section 162 splits fiscal rules neatly across tiers: the National Assembly prescribes how the Federation Account splits among Federal, States, and LGCs (s. 162(3)–(5)), while each State House of Assembly prescribes how the local allocation inside that State is distributed among its local councils (s. 162(8)).
Section 162(8) requires terms prescribed by the State House of Assembly, not unilateral verbal orders.
